summary: Describes an MGCP package for handling endpoints stuck in a lockstep state, in which events are quarantined but not reported, for example after a Call Agent failover during a transient call.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone line gets stuck waiting and never tells anyone what is happening. This gives the controller a way to get it talking again.

subtitle: Detecting and reporting when MGCP endpoints get stuck waiting.

tldr.problem: When a Call Agent fails over during an active call, an MGCP media gateway endpoint can become stuck in a lockstep state where it processes no events but never reports its condition.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a new MGCP Lockstep (LCK) package that lets a Call Agent request endpoints to report if they remain in lockstep state for a specified duration, using a timer and a new RestartInProgress message method.
tldr.outcome: Call Agents can now detect stuck endpoints and take fault recovery procedures, improving reliability in systems with failover.

today: RFC 3992 is an Informational document describing an extension to the non-IETF MGCP protocol, which remains deployed in many VoIP products.

sections.title: Endpoints Getting Stuck
sections.content:
In the Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP), endpoints can enter a lockstep state while waiting for a response to a Notify message and for a subsequent NotificationRequest. During lockstep, an endpoint processes no events and cannot generate new Notifies. Normally this state lasts only briefly.

However, if a Call Agent fails over to a backup during a transient call, an endpoint can be left in lockstep state with no way to notify the new Call Agent of its condition. The endpoint remains stuck, unable to process any new activity, unaware that its original controller is gone.
sections.plainLanguage: When a switch controlling a phone line fails, the phone line might get stuck waiting for instructions that never come. The new switch does not know the phone line is stuck.

sections.title: The Lockstep Package
sections.content:
This RFC defines the LCK (Lockstep) package version 0 with two mechanisms. First, the Call Agent can configure an endpoint with a lockstep timer using the LCK/LST EndpointConfiguration parameter, specifying how long in seconds the endpoint must remain in lockstep before reporting (from 0 to 9999 seconds). A value greater than 2*T-HIST is recommended.

Second, if the lockstep timer expires, the endpoint sends a RestartInProgress (RSIP) message with the LCK/lockstep restart method. This alerts the Call Agent that the endpoint has been stuck. The timer can be audited with the AuditEndpoint command. If the endpoint leaves lockstep before the timer expires, the timer is cancelled.
sections.plainLanguage: The Call Agent tells each phone line 'let me know if you are stuck for more than N seconds'. If the phone line gets stuck that long, it sends a message saying 'I am stuck'.

sections.title: Security and Deployment
sections.content:
Security requirements for the base MGCP protocol in RFC 3435 apply equally to this package. Use of a security protocol such as IPsec that provides per-message authentication and integrity services is required to ensure requests and responses are from authenticated sources and messages have not been modified. Without these services, gateways and Call Agents are open to attacks.

The IESG notes that MGCP itself is a non-IETF protocol currently deployed in many products. Implementers should be aware that RFC 3015 (Megaco, developed in the IETF) is the standards-based way to meet the needs that MGCP addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Make sure messages between the Call Agent and endpoints are encrypted and authenticated so attackers cannot interfere with phone control.
